Onboard Lightweight LLM Reasoning for Human-Aware Safe UAV Navigation

Siwei Cai Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Drexel University, USA. {sc3568, lz457}@drexel.edu    Yuwei Wu Affiliation: GRASP Lab, University of Pennsylvania, USA. {yuweiwu, kumar}@seas.upenn.edu    Vijay Kumar Affiliation: GRASP Lab, University of Pennsylvania, USA. {yuweiwu, kumar}@seas.upenn.edu    Lifeng Zhou ††thanks: †Corresponding author.
Abstract

Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception–planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry—a human-aware safety gap in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8 s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly 3×3\times reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34% to 96%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.

I Introduction

UAVs are increasingly deployed for delivery, inspection, and monitoring in environments shared with people [1, 2, 3]. Such environments are not only dynamic but semantically heterogeneous: a pedestrian, a moving truck, a parked car, and a hedge all constrain the feasible trajectory, yet they imply very different risk and should not receive identical avoidance behavior. Conventional pipelines optimize trajectories well when the environment is accurately modeled [4, 5], but they treat obstacles as geometry: occupancy maps and detections say where an object is, not how it should modify clearance, priority, or motion response [6].

We call the resulting deficiency the human-aware safety gap: a geometric planner assigns a person and a lamp post the same clearance, and its map carries no notion of who or what is being avoided. Human-aware planning should instead maintain larger, category-dependent clearance around people and preserve short-term awareness of them through temporary occlusions. Our goal is therefore not to model people merely as dynamic obstacles, but to preserve category-specific safety semantics when planning around them: closing the gap means producing context-dependent safety constraints—clearance, dynamism, and persistence that depend on the object’s category and the operating context—and delivering them to the planner in real time, onboard.

Large language models (LLMs) offer the abstraction needed to produce such constraints [7, 8], and LLM-based monitoring and planning has begun to appear in robotics [9, 10, 11]. Sinha et al. [9] pair a fast embedding classifier with a slow generative fallback, but the vehicle must wait while the large model reasons; contact-aware planners [11] model interaction physics rather than grounding live observations. Prior landing methods [12, 13] focus on cooperative targets and typically assume obstacle-free landing zones. We ask instead: how can language-based reasoning run onboard an aerial robot so that its understanding of the people and vehicles around it becomes spatially grounded, real-time planner constraints?

Three system-level obstacles stand in the way. (i) LLMs cannot consume raw imagery or 3D geometry, and end-to-end vision-language models (VLMs) are too heavy for Size, Weight and Power (SWaP)-limited platforms [14]; we therefore decouple a light vision-language encoder (VLE) [15] from a text-only LLM and ground its output with depth. (ii) Lightweight LLMs that fit onboard hallucinate [16]; we stabilize them with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [17] over a safety knowledge base and constrain decoding to a JSON grammar. (iii) Semantic guidance must not break real-time control; the LLM never commands the vehicle but adjusts planner-level constraints (unsafe regions and margins) consumed by a model-based planner and controller. A fourth obstacle emerged only after closed-loop deployment among pedestrians: with a 2 s map decay, a brief occlusion removes a person’s constraint from the map before they reappear, so the pipeline needs object persistence in addition to semantics.

This paper contributes: (1) a semantic-to-spatial grounding pipeline that turns RGB-D observations into obstacle-specific risk and 3D safety constraints; (2) a RAG-stabilized, grammar-constrained lightweight LLM reasoning module, whose per-class verdicts are cached so that the LLM reasons once per category rather than per frame, with a cache-miss reasoning pathway for categories outside a fixed semantic policy; (3) persistent obstacle identities with occlusion-aware holding in the planner map; and (4) an onboard feasibility study on Jetson-class hardware together with closed-loop Gazebo experiments in urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles and in autonomous landing, with an analysis of perception under the limited input resolution that onboard compute imposes.

II Method

Fig.  shows the three subsystems. Perception converts RGB-D frames into semantic and spatial primitives; Reasoning maps them to obstacle-specific safety parameters; Action keeps a persistent obstacle set and injects it into a model-based planner.

II-A Perception: Shared VLE, Segmentation, and 3D Grounding

A single frozen BLIP ViT-B/16 encoder [15] (≈\approx86M parameters) serves two heads, avoiding redundant visual computation onboard. The captioning branch is BLIP’s original decoder and yields a short zero-shot scene description (≈30{\approx}30 tokens) that identifies potential hazards. The segmentation head is a lightweight decoder we train on top of the encoder: multi-scale features from layers LL, L/2L/2, and L/4L/4 are projected to a common width with 1×11{\times}1 convolutions and fused via skip connections [18]; a text prompt (e.g., “person”, “car”) conditions the fused map 𝐅vis\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{vis}} through FiLM [19],

𝐅cond=𝐅vis⊙(1+γ⁡(𝐞text))+β⁡(𝐞text),\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{cond}}=\mathbf{F}_{\mathrm{vis}}\odot\big(1+\gamma(\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{text}})\big)+\beta(\mathbf{e}_{\mathrm{text}}), (1)

before four resize-convolution up-blocks (bilinear upsampling followed by a 3×33{\times}3 convolution, which avoids checkerboard artifacts [20]) produce the mask ℳ\mathcal{M}. Each connected component of ℳ\mathcal{M} that exceeds an area threshold is back-projected through the time-aligned depth map with intrinsics 𝐊\mathbf{K},

𝐏center=1|ℳ|​∑(u,v)∈ℳZu,v​𝐊−1​[u,v, 1]⊤,\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{center}}=\tfrac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|}\textstyle\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{M}}Z_{u,v}\,\mathbf{K}^{-1}[u,\,v,\,1]^{\top}, (2)

after rejecting depths more than 2​σ2\sigma from the in-mask median. The result is a list of (class,𝐏center,confidence)(\text{class},\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{center}},\text{confidence}) tuples at 10 Hz.

II-B Reasoning: From Semantics to Safety Parameters

LLM-populated verdict cache. The LLM does not run per frame; it runs per class. The first time a class label appears, its name and the scene caption are sent through retrieval and the LLM, which returns a semantic verdict {is_dynamic,bbox_size}\{\texttt{is\_dynamic},\texttt{bbox\_size}\}; the verdict is stored in a per-class cache and reused for every later detection of that class at no inference cost. The cache is therefore not a hand-written lookup table but the accumulated output of the reasoning module: it is warm-started with the verdicts the same RAG–LLM path produced for the categories the segmentation head is prompted with (person, car, truck), and it grows whenever a new label is encountered. This mechanism is designed to extend the pipeline beyond a fixed semantic policy: labels absent from the cache can trigger retrieval-grounded reasoning and subsequently be handled like cached categories. In our 20-run urban benchmark, however, every observed label hit the warm cache, so no online LLM query was issued after initialization; the landing ablation in Sec. IV-B isolates the contribution of the reasoning path itself. In our 20-run urban benchmark every label hit the warm cache, so no online LLM query was issued after initialization; the landing ablation in Sec. IV-B isolates the contribution of the reasoning path itself. Because a novel object can appear at any moment, the full stack is loaded at start-up rather than lazily, and a verdict that fails grammar validation falls back to a conservative default box rather than discarding the object.

Hybrid retrieval. For an unknown class, the caption and class name query a local safety knowledge base (KB) with a hybrid search: dense retrieval (bge-small-en-v1.5, <100{<}100 MB) captures synonyms (“pedestrian”→\rightarrow“person”), while sparse BM25 anchors high-priority keywords (“truck”). Scores are fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion [21], S⁡(d)=∑m1/(η+rm​(d))S(d)=\sum_{m}1/(\eta+r_{m}(d)), η=60\eta{=}60, and only the top-kk segments enter the prompt to avoid attention dilution in small models [22].

Edge inference and grammar-constrained output. Reasoning runs Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct on llama.cpp with importance-matrix 4-bit quantization [23] and a statically allocated KV cache for constant memory and predictable latency. A GBNF grammar restricts decoding to the expected {"is_dynamic": yes|no, "bbox_size": float} schema, which substantially reduces malformed generations and removes the need for a separate free-form parsing stage. Following Code as Policies [24], the LLM is deliberately restricted to semantic risk (dynamic or not, how much clearance) and does not produce waypoints: small models are poor at Euclidean arithmetic [25], and encoding dense geometry into the prompt inflates context and degrades reasoning [26].

II-C Action: Persistent Obstacles and Planner Constraints

Persistent identity and occlusion hold. A per-frame detection list is not enough for planning near people: temporary occlusions (e.g., a pedestrian passing behind a parked vehicle) create gaps in detections, and with a fixed voxel decay the corresponding constraint leaves the map within seconds, motivating short-term persistence in the planner map. We assign each detection a stable object id by greedy nearest-neighbor association within its class (gate 22 m, time-to-live 44 s) and publish the semantic box together with that id. The planner map keeps, per id, the last-seen time and last known box; an object whose age is below a hold time ThT_{h} (3 s) stays in the map at its last position, and only afterwards are its voxels released. Holding in place rather than extrapolating is deliberate for pedestrians, whose heading is not persistent; vehicles can be extrapolated with a tracked velocity when available. Human awareness thus enters the planner through differentiated clearance and persistence policies rather than by treating people as generic occupied space. Ids also expose a metric we use in Sec. IV: how many objects are carried across detection gaps.

Unsafe regions in the planner. Every dynamic object yields an axis-aligned box ℬi\mathcal{B}_{i} of side bbox_size around 𝐏center\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{center}}; the unsafe set is ℬ=⋃iℬi\mathcal{B}=\bigcup_{i}\mathcal{B}_{i}. The planner interface is intentionally minimal so that the back end can be swapped. For the landing case study we follow [27]: a kinodynamic A* front end whose heuristic is augmented with a soft penalty h~​(𝐩)=h0​(𝐩)+λ​ϕ​(𝐩)\tilde{h}(\mathbf{p})=h_{0}(\mathbf{p})+\lambda\,\phi(\mathbf{p}), where ϕ\phi grows quadratically with penetration into ℬ\mathcal{B} and states inside ℬ\mathcal{B} are pruned, followed by a nonlinear MPC whose safe-flight corridor 𝒫~c⊆𝒫c\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{c}\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{c} is regenerated with 𝒫~c∩ℬ=∅\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_{c}\cap\mathcal{B}=\emptyset, and an S​E​(3)SE(3) geometric controller [28] for tracking. For the urban navigation experiments the same boxes are injected as inflated voxels into the ESDF-free grid map of a B-spline local planner (EGO-Planner [29]), demonstrating that the semantic layer is planner-agnostic.

III Onboard Feasibility

Why not the cloud. Field radio telemetry gives us ≈100{\approx}100 kbps uplink, so a single 384×384384{\times}384 JPEG (≈800{\approx}800 kbit) costs ≈8{\approx}8 s to transmit; measured JSON-generation latency of hosted models adds 1.61.6–2.82.8 s on average with spikes above 4.74.7 s (GPT-3.5-Turbo/GPT-4o/GPT-5.1-low: 1.62/2.80/2.42 s). A roughly 1010 s round trip could correspond to about 10 m of travel at 11 m/s before a semantic result is available. Everything therefore runs onboard.

Platform. We compared an Intel NUC 13 Pro (CPU only, >40{>}40 W, 256 g decased), a Jetson Orin Nano (8 GB, 15 W), and a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB, 25 W, 100 TOPS, ≈180{\approx}180 g with carrier). The decased NUC weighs 256 g, compared with approximately 180 g for the Orin NX with carrier, draws more than 40 W, and lacks tensor cores; in our implementation the 8 GB Orin Nano could not accommodate the VLE, KB, LLM, VIO, and ROS stack simultaneously. We deploy on the Orin NX.

Modular VLE+LLM versus monolithic small VLMs. Monolithic small VLMs project an image into 144–576 visual tokens that must traverse the full language backbone, and rely on 300–675M-parameter encoders. Our “compress-then-reason” design sends ≈30{\approx}30 text tokens through a 0.5B model behind an 86M encoder, reducing the number of language-model input tokens by more than 19×19\times relative to the compared monolithic VLMs (Table I); the same encoder output is reused by the segmentation head.

LLM selection. We benchmarked Llama-3.1/3.2, Qwen-2.5, Gemma-2 and Phi-3.5 families at Q3–FP16 on the Orin NX for peak memory, generation time, and instruction following (valid JSON without filler). Gemma-2, Phi-3.5, and aggressively quantized Llama-3.2-1B (IQ4, Q3) frequently failed to follow the required output schema under the tested quantization settings; Llama-3.1-8B fits in memory but exceeds 3.33.3 s per query. Qwen-2.5-0.5B (Q4_K_M) answers in ≈0.75{\approx}0.75–0.790.79 s using 5.65.6 GB of total system memory, leaving headroom for perception and VIO; on the desktop-class simulation host the same call takes 0.210.21–0.410.41 s. With the per-class verdict cache of Sec. II-B this latency is incurred once per new category rather than per frame; the perception loop maintained 9.969.96 Hz over 20 runs.

IV Experiments

All closed-loop experiments use ROS Noetic with Gazebo physics and simulated RGB-D sensing [30]. The primary evaluation is low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles (Sec. IV-A), the setting that motivated the human-aware safety gap and where the persistence mechanism was introduced (EGO-Planner back end); autonomous landing (Sec. IV-B) serves as a second case study with the kinodynamic-A*/MPC back end.

IV-A Urban Navigation Among Pedestrians and Vehicles

Setup. A town world contains two scripted SUVs (one crossing the UAV’s path head-on, one emerging from behind a wall at 1.5–2 m/s) and two walkers (one along the road at 1.2 m/s, one performing a bounded random walk at 1 m/s). The UAV flies a fixed multi-goal route at low altitude for ≈106{\approx}106 s; the perception front end runs the fixed prompt set {person, car, truck} at 10 Hz. We compare the geometric planner (off) against the full semantic pipeline with persistent ids and Th=3T_{h}{=}3 s (on), 20 runs each with identical goals and spawn points.

Closed-loop safety. Collision events per run drop from 1.351.35 to 0.450.45 (p=0.038p{=}0.038), the only safety metric that reaches significance at n=20n{=}20; worst-case clearance improves in mean (0.16→0.520.16\rightarrow 0.52 m) but not significantly, and crash counts (3 vs. 1 of 20) are within noise. The semantic planner maintains larger human-aware separation through additional detours, at the cost of path length (54.5→68.754.5\rightarrow 68.7 m) and peak jerk (2.6×2.6\times). The simulator is not deterministic; with a per-run worst-clearance standard deviation of 0.50.5–0.80.8 m, differences below ≈0.2{\approx}0.2 m are not resolvable at n=20n{=}20.

Persistence and the verdict cache. Per run, an average of 45 object ids are created, 23% of which die after a single frame (background artifacts); 23 survive at least 11 s, and 20 are carried across a detection gap of ≥0.5{\geq}0.5 s, with the longest bridged gap equal to the 44 s time-to-live and single ids surviving up to 7070 s. All observed classes were served from the warm verdict cache during these runs, so no online LLM query was issued, and perception maintained 9.969.96 Hz.

IV-B Case Study: Semantics-Aware Landing

Setup and baselines. Three environments (Fig. 2) test generalization; the open field additionally contains a humanoid walking unpredictably near the landing pad. A trial succeeds if the UAV lands within 0.5 m of the target without entering the actor’s 1 m safety buffer (50 trials per cell). We compare (i) Baseline MPC, the same planner with depth-only geometric avoidance; (ii) LLM–MPC, the LLM acting on BLIP captions without RAG; and (iii) Ours, the full RAG-stabilized pipeline.

Results. Table II shows that geometric avoidance alone reaches 34% among moving actors because it cannot anticipate that a pedestrian requires a larger, earlier safety margin than a static object, while the unaugmented LLM is worse than no LLM at all (6–12%): hallucinated or malformed verdicts destabilize the planner. RAG plus grammar-constrained decoding turns the same 0.5B model into a reliable source of safety constraints.

IV-C Perception Under Limited Input Resolution

The 224-pixel encoder input limits the effective resolution available for small, distant objects. This effect is most noticeable for pedestrians, which occupy a much smaller image area than vehicles at the same range. The larger pedestrian margin and short-term persistence help maintain conservative safety behavior under this sensing limitation. We therefore use a larger pedestrian safety margin and preserve pedestrian-specific constraints through short occlusions. Higher-resolution perception within the same onboard compute budget is left for future work.

V Conclusion

We showed that a 0.5B-parameter LLM, grounded by retrieval, constrained to a machine-parseable schema, kept off the per-frame critical path by per-class verdict caching, and complemented by object persistence in the planner map, can supply context-dependent safety constraints for aerial robots operating around people: a pedestrian and a parked car receive different clearance, and pedestrian-specific constraints persist through short occlusions. The full stack runs on a Jetson Orin NX, reduces collision events roughly threefold in urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles—at the cost of longer paths and sharper maneuvers—and raises landing success among moving actors from 34% to 96%. In the evaluated closed-loop scenarios, all observed categories were served from the warm verdict cache; evaluating retrieval-grounded reasoning for previously unseen categories, including comparison against fixed semantic policies, remains future work. Small-object perception at range is another remaining limitation, primarily due to the 224-pixel encoder input. Future work will therefore investigate higher-resolution perception within the same compute budget, improved per-class motion models for persistent objects, and cache-miss reasoning for novel categories.
